title: continuous-batching-scheduler-tuning-experiments-11
content:
TL;DR:
We ran a focused set of continuous-batching scheduler experiments to explore trade-offs between max batch size, max-wait timeout, and fairness policies with the primary goal of reducing p99 tail latency without sacrificing aggregate throughput. Key findings: a moderate max-wait (4–6ms) with adaptive max-batch sizing (min 2, max 16) and request-priority-aware fairness yields the best p95/p99 improvement (~12–18% p99 reduction) with negligible throughput loss on our 8xA100 serving cluster. Aggressive timeouts (>=10ms) reduce throughput variance but increase average latency and hurt p50.

Background / Motivation:
We have observed intermittent p99 spikes under realistic mixed workloads (short chat-turn queries + occasional long completions). Continuous batching can amortize kernel overheads, but naive batching parameters drive tail latency regressions for low-QPS tenants. This doc captures experiments to tune: max_batch_size, max_wait_ms (scheduler window), fairness policy (FIFO vs age-based vs priority-aware), and aggressive tail-protection heuristics.

Goals / Success metrics:
- Primary: reduce p99 token latency across mixed workload scenarios by >=10% compared to baseline config (mbs=32, wait=8ms, FIFO).
- Secondary: keep p50 within +20% of baseline, and maintain >=95% of baseline throughput (tokens/s) for steady-state traffic.
- Operational: ensure config is stable (no oscillation) and easy to express in route configs.

Testbed / Setup:
- Code baseline: serving-runtime main @ PR 341 (linked) with continuous-batching + improved metrics hooks.
- Hardware: 4 nodes x 2xA100 (80GB) (i.e., 8 GPUs total).
- Models: mix of two model families to represent heterogeneity: small chat model (7B, relatively cheap) and medium long-completion model (13B). Both quantized (4-bit) with KV-cache enabled.
- Traffic generator: replay traces from prod-sim (mixed QPS profile: 70% short-turns, 30% long completions). Injected synthetic bursts to simulate tail events (sudden 5x QPS for 2s every 60s).
- Metrics captured: p50/p90/p95/p99 token latency, tokens/s throughput, effective batch size distribution, batch wait distribution, GPU utilization, queue lengths, and fairness delta (measured as difference in latency percentiles between high- and low-priority tenants).
- Duration: each run = 30 minutes steady-state + 5 burst cycles; results aggregated over final 20 minutes.

Experiment matrix (high level):
A. Baseline: max_batch_size=32, max_wait_ms=8, fairness=FIFO
B. Small batches: mbs=8, max_wait=4ms, FIFO
C. Adaptive batch: mbs range [2,16], wait=6ms, FIFO
D. Priority-aware fairness: same as C but fairness=priority (short-turns prioritized), with starvation protection (max-age=50ms)
E. Age-based fairness: mbs [2,16], wait=6ms, fairness=age-based (older requests first)
F. Aggressive timeout: mbs=32, wait=12ms, FIFO (control for latency variance)

Key results summary (aggregated):
- Baseline (A): p50=12.6ms, p95=68.3ms, p99=220.1ms, throughput=~185k tokens/s, effective_batch_mean=19.
- B (small batches): p50=10.8ms (better), p95=72.5ms (slightly worse), p99=260.3ms (worse), throughput=150k tokens/s (drop ~19%) — reason: lost batching efficiency, more kernel invocations, lower GPU utilization.
- C (adaptive): p50=11.9ms, p95=60.2ms, p99=195.7ms (~11% p99 improvement vs baseline), throughput=178k tokens/s (~96% of baseline), effective_batch_mean=12 (more stable distribution).
- D (priority-aware): p50=11.5ms, p95=55.0ms, p99=180.5ms (~18% p99 improvement), throughput=176k tokens/s, fairness delta reduced by ~40% (low-priority latency improved at cost of modest high-priority p50 increase). Starvation protection events rare (<0.5% requests).
- E (age-based): p50=12.1ms, p95=62.8ms, p99=202.9ms (marginal improvement), throughput=176k tokens/s. Age-based helps reduce worst-case starvation but less effective than priority-aware when short-turns dominate.
- F (aggressive timeout): p50=14.2ms (worse), p95=58.1ms, p99=190.4ms, throughput=182k tokens/s. Higher wait helps tail but raises avg latency.

Interpretation / Observations:
- Adaptive batching (C) hits a good balance: smaller max batch cap reduces added latency for short requests but still allows batching in bursts. It preserves most throughput while improving tail.
- Priority-aware fairness (D) yields the best tail gains because it avoids long requests from blocking short ones. The max-age starvation protection is critical; without it we observed low-priority requests starve during long tails.
- Aggressive small batches (B) degrade throughput too much — not acceptable for hosted API economics.
- Increasing max_wait beyond ~8–10ms reduces p99 in some cases but increases p50 significantly and hurts latency-sensitive SLAs. The sweet spot we observed is 4–6ms when combined with adaptive batch caps and priority-aware fairness.
- Effective batch size distribution matters more than mean: heavy tail in batch sizes correlates with p99 spikes. Limiting max batch size reduces variance.

Operational considerations / Safety:
- Starvation protection: always keep max_age or a token-based bypass to handle long-wait requests. Configurable per-route.
- Telemetry: we need new per-route metrics: mean & p99 batch wait, per-priority p99, starvation_count, and recent-starvation-window. These were added in PR 341 but dashboarding still incomplete (linked artifact).
- Rollout plan: roll C+D as a canary on 10% of hosted routes for 48 hours with auto-revert if p99 increases by >5% or throughput drops >10%.

Recommendations (short):
1) Default scheduler config for hosted API: adaptive_batch_range=[2,16], max_wait_ms=6, fairness=priority_with_starvation_protection(max_age_ms=50).
2) Add per-route overrides for strict latency SLAs (allow max_wait_ms=3 and mbs cap=8) and for high-throughput routes (allow mbs up to 32 with longer wait).
3) Dashboard: add batch-wait and per-priority latency charts; set alerts on starvation_count > 1% over 10m.
4) Follow-up experiments: explore model-aware batching (separate batch pools per model-size), and dynamic wait tuning using short-term queue depth prediction.

Unresolved questions / TODOs:
- How does this generalize to Dedicated private deployments where GPU counts are much larger — do we need different defaults? (TODO: run 16-GPU cluster experiments).
- Evaluate interaction with KV-cache warmup (long completions cause bigger KV cache churn); we saw hints of compound effects on p99.
- More stress testing with multi-tenant isolation cases (one tenant with bursty traffic should not degrade others).

Commands / notes to reproduce (approx):
- Traffic replay: tools/replay/run --trace prod-sim-202511 --duration 40m --burst-pattern periodic --scale 1.0
- Scheduler config prototype: configs/scheduler/experimental/priority-adaptive-6ms.yaml (attached to PR 341)
- Perf harness: tools/bench/collect-metrics --job-id cbatch-20251111 --out s3://redwood-bench/cbatch/20251111

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working doc; numbers are median of 3 runs for each config and represent our early conclusions. Please review the rollout thresholds and the proposed default route config.
- Related: see Jira INF-4821 for customer-reported p99 incidents and linked PR for instrumentation.
